parts: A king feels that he would never fail if he knew three things: the right time to begin everything, the right people to listen to (and whom to avoid), and the most important thing to do. He offers a great reward to anyone who can answer.

Learned men give different answers. For the first question: draw up a timetable and keep to it; watch everything and not waste time on idle pleasures; consult a council of wise men; ask magicians. For the second: councillors, priests, doctors or warriors. For the third: science, skill in warfare, or religious worship. The king is not satisfied.

He decides to consult a hermit famous for his wisdom, who sees only simple folk. The king dresses as an ordinary man, leaves his bodyguard behind and walks to the hut. The hermit, frail and breathing heavily, is digging beds and does not answer. The king takes the spade and digs for hours.

At sunset a bearded man runs out of the wood, bleeding from a stomach wound, and faints. The king washes and bandages the wound and gives him water; tired out, he sleeps on the threshold. In the morning the man confesses that he is the king's enemy: the king had executed his brother and seized his property, and he had come to kill the king on his way back. The king's bodyguard had wounded him. Now he begs forgiveness and promises to serve the king faithfully. The king forgives him, promises to restore his property and to send his doctor.

The hermit then says the king has had his answers. Had he not stayed to dig, the man would have attacked him: so the most important time was when he was digging, the hermit was the most important man, and doing him good was the most important business. Later the wounded man was the most important person. Remember, he says, there is only one important time — Now, the only time we have power. The most important person is the one you are with, and the most important affair is to do him good.

Leo (Lev Nikolayevich) Tolstoy wrote it in Russian; it was published in What Men Live By, and Other Tales (1903), translated by the Maudes. It is a parable — a short story with human characters that teaches a moral.
Themes: living in the present, kindness and service, forgiveness turning an enemy into a friend.

Forming questions: yes/no questions (auxiliary + subject + verb), wh-questions (wh-word + auxiliary + subject + verb), questions with modals (Can/May/Should …), negative questions (Didn't you …?). Antonyms (persuade/dissuade, success/failure).
